pages.title: Plato's Theory of Justice: Cephalus and Polemarchus
pages.summary: Justice is introduced as the core concern of political philosophy and Plato's book. Plato critiques Cephalus's view of paying dues and Polemarchus's idea of harming enemies, arguing justice must be universal and good to all.

pages.title: Thrasymachus's View on Justice and Plato's Counterargument
pages.summary: Thrasymachus argues that justice is the interest of the stronger, meaning might is right and laws serve the powerful. Plato counters that laws benefit everyone, obeying them is a duty, and a lawbreaker's soul is never satisfied.

pages.title: Glaucon's Contractual Theory and Principles of Justice
pages.summary: Glaucon presents justice as the interest of the weak through a contractual state, which Plato counters by asserting the state serves all. The discussion concludes that justice is a duty and virtue promoting peace, harmony, and welfare for everyone.

pages.title: Plato's Idea of Justice and the State
pages.summary: Plato seeks God's idea of justice through the soul, defining a just person as one dominated by reason with non-interfering elements living in peace. He posits that the state is individual writ large, reflecting the soul's three elements in three classes.

pages.title: Three Classes of the State and Criticisms
pages.summary: Plato divides the state into ruling, soldier, and producer classes based on soul qualities, arguing proper stationing and non-interference yield harmony and excellence. However, this ideal state is criticized as impracticable today, drawing comparisons to how the varna system deteriorated.

pages.title: The State as Individual Writ Large
pages.summary: Plato explains that the state is an abstraction inhering in the minds of its people, functioning as a magnified version of the individual. Consequently, justice in the individual applies to the state, creating continuity between ethics and politics.

pages.title: Plato's Theory of Education and Greek Influences
pages.summary: Plato designs education to determine personal aptitude and establish the ideal state, combining Spartan state control and gender equality with Athenian intellectual development. His curriculum begins with primary education consisting of gymnastics, music, and moral stories.

pages.title: Stages of Education and the Philosopher King
pages.summary: Plato's educational scheme includes secondary education, compulsory military training, and higher education with screening tests that assign individuals to social classes. Those completing studies by age fifty become philosophers who reluctantly accept kingship out of civic obligation.

pages.title: Philosopher Kings as Rulers and Athens Governance
pages.summary: Plato diagnoses Athens's problems as the rule of ignorance and proposes that philosopher kings, who lack lust for power, should rule reluctantly. The notes conclude that while Plato's diagnosis is accurate, relying on reluctant rulers is a flawed prescription for governance.

pages.title: Plato's Theory of Communism of Property and Family
pages.summary: Plato proposes communism of property and family exclusively for the guardian class to prevent corruption and nepotism. The state acts as a single family and regulates marriages between the ablest men and women for eugenic purposes.

pages.title: Plato on Marriage and Aristotle on Property
pages.summary: This page outlines the purpose of marriage and state child custody in Plato's Republic alongside criticisms of his communism. It also details Aristotle's defense of private property as a source of motivation, recognition, order, and charity.

pages.title: Aristotle on Family and Plato's Philosopher King
pages.summary: Aristotle criticizes Plato's communism of family, asserting that family is necessary for emotional stability and that both property and family are time-tested institutions. The page also introduces the philosopher king, detailing the qualifications, absolute powers, and single constitutional limitation of this ruler.

pages.title: Philosopher King's Powers and Aristotle's Criticism
pages.summary: This page discusses the justification for the absolute powers of Plato's philosopher king, whose supreme knowledge should not be limited by public opinion. It concludes with Aristotle's critique, which advocates for the rule of law because philosopher kings are impossible to find, fallible to appetite, and law embodies collective wisdom.

pages.title: Aristotle on Law and Plato Versus Marx
pages.summary: Aristotle argues that the rule of law is the best practicable system, supporting checks and balances against absolute power. The page then evaluates Plato as a communist, noting superficial similarities with Karl Marx regarding class and property, alongside fundamental philosophical differences between idealism and materialism.

pages.title: Plato Versus Marx and Plato as Fascist
pages.summary: This page contrasts Plato and Karl Marx across class basis, class relations, the role of the state, and methods of change like education versus violent revolution. It also introduces the evaluation of Plato as a fascist, defining fascism and totalitarianism through historical regimes requiring complete subservience to the state.

flashcards.front: How does Plato refute Cephalus's definition of justice as paying one's dues?
flashcards.back: Plato argues that returning a borrowed weapon to a friend who has gone mad cannot be considered just. Since this rule cannot be applied in all circumstances, paying one's dues cannot serve as a universal principle of justice.

flashcards.front: What is Thrasymachus's formulation of justice, and how does Plato counter it?
flashcards.back: Thrasymachus asserts that justice is the interest of the stronger, meaning might is right and laws reflect rulers' self-interest. Plato counters that the laws of the state exist for the welfare and benefit of all, making obedience a moral duty.

flashcards.front: How does Glaucon explain the origin of justice, and what is Plato's objection?
flashcards.back: Glaucon presents a contractual theory where the weak come together to form the state for their mutual protection, making justice the interest of the weak. Plato objects by arguing that the state is not meant solely for the weak, but exists in the interest of all.

flashcards.front: What does Plato mean by the philosophical aphorism that 'state is individual writ large'?
flashcards.back: Plato asserts that the state is a magnified version of the individual, differing only like large letters and small letters. States do not emerge from oak or rock but inhere in the minds of the people living within them.

flashcards.front: Why did Rousseau characterize Plato's Republic as the greatest work on education?
flashcards.back: Plato treated education exhaustively as the primary method to identify human aptitudes and establish the ideal state. His holistic curriculum systematically synthesizes the state-sponsored physical discipline of Sparta with the intellectual and critical development of Athens.

flashcards.front: How does the screening process operate across the stages of Plato's education system?
flashcards.back: Students who fail the first screening at age 18 enter the producer class, while those lacking aptitude for higher dialectics after military training at age 20 join the soldier class. The remaining candidates study philosophy and undergo practical training until age 50 to qualify as philosopher rulers.

flashcards.front: Why does Plato advocate that states are best governed when rulers are reluctant to govern?
flashcards.back: Plato contends that philosophers love knowledge rather than power or material wealth, meaning they will not misuse their authority for corruption. They accept political rule only reluctantly out of civic obligation to the state rather than selfish ambition.

flashcards.front: Why does Plato institute the communism of family exclusively for the guardian class?
flashcards.back: Plato considers the private family a greater source of corruption and nepotism than property. He restricts family communism to guardians to liberate women for state duties and conduct state-regulated selective mating for eugenic improvement.

flashcards.front: What arguments does Aristotle advance against Plato's abolition of private property?
flashcards.back: Aristotle argues that private property provides essential motivation, personal recognition, and the means for practicing charity. Moreover, property owners possess reason and maintain a tangible stake in the preservation of social order and stability.

flashcards.front: Why does Aristotle advocate the rule of law over Plato's institution of the philosopher king?
flashcards.back: Aristotle argues that finding an ideal philosopher king is impossible, and even an enlightened ruler possesses human appetites that could corrupt absolute power. In contrast, law represents collective wisdom and the wisdom of ages, offering a more dependable and practicable foundation for governance.

answers.question: Examine Plato's theory of justice. How does he establish that the state is individual writ large?
answers.intro: Plato places justice as the central concern of political philosophy in his book Republic, subtitled 'Concerning Justice'. He rejects conventional views through dialectics to establish justice as an internal soul virtue reflected outward in the state.
body: Through dialectics, Plato rejects Cephalus's view of returning borrowed weapons to a madman and Polemarchus's formula of harming enemies, establishing with Gandhi-like ethics that justice never harms anyone.
Plato refutes Thrasymachus's sophist claim that might is right and Glaucon's contractual theory that justice serves only the weak, asserting instead that state laws serve the common welfare of all.
Justifying that the state is individual writ large, Plato argues states do not arise from oak or rock but inhere in human minds, reflecting individual soul elements on a larger political canvas.

The tripartite soul dominated by reason, courage, or appetite corresponds directly to the ruling, soldier, and producer classes, where justice is defined as proper stationing and non-interference among classes.

While this functional specialization promotes harmony and excellence, the notes observe that such rigid social stratification historically risked deteriorating from a division of labour into a division of labourers, like the varna system.
answers.conclusion: Plato establishes vital continuity between individual ethics and state politics. Nonetheless, as the notes conclude, Plato's ideal state proves undesirable in practice because excellence cannot be the sole principle of justice without accommodating human realities.

answers.question: Critically evaluate Plato's institution of the philosopher king. Can absolute power be justified on grounds of superior knowledge?
answers.intro: Plato prescribes the rule of the philosopher king as the ultimate solution to ignorance and corruption in Athens. He asserts that no law or ordinance is mightier than knowledge, granting the philosopher ruler unconstrained authority.
body: Plato justifies absolute governance by arguing that philosophers possess true knowledge of the good life, undergo fifty years of rigorous education, and remain devoid of lust for property, family, or power.

Defending unrestricted power, Plato contends that limiting an enlightened ruler with written laws or public opinion is as foolish as restricting an expert practitioner of medicine with a book of medicine, leaving only the constitution unalterable.

Aristotle strongly criticizes this ideal, arguing that philosopher kings are impossible to find and remain fallible humans whose appetite may eventually overwhelm reason, whereas laws embody the dependable collective wisdom of ages.

Aristotle cautions that Plato sacrifices the achievable good for an unachievable best, maintaining that while philosopher rule might be ideal, the rule of law represents the best practicable system for governance.

The critique is reinforced by Lord Acton's principle that power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely, demonstrating why institutional checks and balances are preferable to relying on the unchecked virtue of an individual.
answers.conclusion: Plato accurately diagnoses that governance requires wisdom and integrity, yet his prescription of absolutism remains flawed. As Aristotle proves, enduring governance relies on the rule of law and checks and balances rather than unchecked individuals.
